reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline pathogenic variants in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumour-suppressor genes, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with high but incomplete penetrance
Confers markedly raised lifetime risks of breast and ovarian (including fallopian tube and primary peritoneal) cancer, often at younger ages than sporadic disease
BRCA1 is associated with triple-negative and high-grade breast cancers, whereas BRCA2 also raises the risk of male breast cancer, prostate cancer and pancreatic cancer

Suspect the syndrome with early-onset breast cancer, bilateral disease, ovarian cancer at any age, male breast cancer, or clustering in the family, and note enrichment in Ashkenazi Jewish founder populations
Surveillance combines annual breast MRI with mammography, and risk-reducing options include risk-reducing mastectomy and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy
BRCA-mutated cancers show defective homologous-recombination repair and are sensitive to PARP inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapy
Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy also lowers breast cancer risk when performed premenopausally and reduces ovarian cancer mortality
reference.pathophysiology: BRCA1 and BRCA2 encode proteins essential for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, a high-fidelity mechanism that preserves genomic integrity. A germline loss-of-function variant leaves cells dependent on error-prone repair pathways, and loss of the remaining functional allele in breast or ovarian epithelium removes homologous-recombination capacity entirely. The resulting genomic instability accelerates the accumulation of oncogenic mutations, while this same repair deficiency is the vulnerability exploited therapeutically by PARP inhibition through synthetic lethality.
additionalDifferentials: PALB2, CHEK2 and ATM moderate-penetrance breast cancer predisposition
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with breast and gynaecological risk
Sporadic early-onset breast or ovarian cancer without an identifiable germline variant
additionalInvestigations: Germline BRCA1/BRCA2 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, usually within a multigene panel
Annual breast MRI supplemented by mammography from a risk-appropriate age
Clinical breast examination and structured risk counselling
Discussion of risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy timing with pelvic assessment where surgery is deferred
Tumour homologous-recombination-deficiency or somatic BRCA testing to guide targeted therapy
Consideration of prostate and pancreatic surveillance in relevant BRCA2 carriers
redFlags: A new breast mass, skin change or nipple abnormality in a carrier
Abdominal distension, bloating or pelvic symptoms suggesting ovarian malignancy
Breast cancer in a male carrier
Rapidly progressive symptoms indicating advanced or metastatic disease
reference.prognosis: Lifetime breast and ovarian cancer risks are substantial but modifiable, and risk-reducing surgery greatly lowers incidence and mortality. Because effective surveillance and targeted therapies such as PARP inhibitors exist, early identification of carriers meaningfully improves outcomes.
pitfalls: Testing only for founder variants and missing other pathogenic changes across the genes
Relying on mammography alone and omitting breast MRI in high-risk surveillance
Deferring discussion of risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy given the lack of effective ovarian screening
Failing to offer cascade testing to male relatives and to at-risk family members
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
NCCN Guidelines: Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment - Breast, Ovarian and Pancreatic
